In learning the Buddha’s teachings, what matters most is true practice and true realization, resolving birth and death and escaping the round of rebirth. Therefore one must first subdue the afflictions, and then cut them off. In the Great Sutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness the Buddha sets forth in concrete and detailed terms how to subdue the afflictions and how to cut them off: the continuous awareness and contemplation of the arising and ceasing, the changes, of body, mind, and world — this is the most simple and direct method leading from knowing suffering to ending suffering. Practicing as taught, one is able to:
“Cultivating the state in which there is only awareness and contemplation, one transcends clinging and no longer craves or hates anything in body, mind, or world.”

When the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, his disciples unanimously asked Ānanda to put the question: “While the Buddha dwelt in the world, we dwelt relying on the Buddha; when the Buddha has entered cessation, on what shall we dwell?” The Buddha replied:
“After I enter cessation, you bhikkhus should dwell
(the four foundations of mindfulness are also called the four abidings of mindfulness)
in the four foundations of mindfulness.”
Moreover, at the very beginning of this sutta the Buddha said:

“Bhikkhus! There is only one path that can purify sentient beings, overcome sorrow and lamentation, extinguish suffering and grief, practice the truth, and realize nirvāṇa — and that path is the four foundations of mindfulness.”
Therefore the Great Sutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness (that is, the Great Sutta on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness) is a treasure of practice of the utmost importance.

[One should dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness] In order to still the deluded thoughts and to make the mind correct rather than crooked, pure and undefiled, one settles the mind on the four foundations:
either the foundation of mindfulness of body
(settling the mind on the body: either observing the breath, or observing movements, or observing impermanence, or observing impurity, or observing the four great elements, or observing a corpse),
or the foundation of mindfulness of feeling
(settling the mind on feeling: observing feelings),
or the foundation of mindfulness of mind
(settling the mind on mind: observing the mind),
or the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena

(settling the mind on phenomena: either observing the five hindrances, or observing the five aggregates, or observing the faculties and their objects, or observing the seven factors of enlightenment, or observing the Four Noble Truths).

The Sutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness appears twice in the Pali Sutta Piṭaka of the Theravāda tradition. According to the Pali Text Society’s English translation of the Pali canon: once in the Dīgha Nikāya as sutta 22, and once in the Majjhima Nikāya as sutta 10, the two suttas being identical in content. The Dīgha Nikāya sutta 22, however, expounds the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena at greater length than the Majjhima Nikāya sutta 10, and so it is called the Great Sutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness, while the Majjhima Nikāya sutta 10 is called the Sutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness. The word nian (mindfulness) in both titles, “Great Sutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness” and “Sutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness,” means awareness and contemplation with right mindfulness.

[Right mindfulness] Correct thoughts. To give rise to no wrong thoughts and to recollect the right path is called “right mindfulness.” [Foundation of mindfulness] Through mindful awareness and contemplation, one gathers in the mind and settles it on one point. The Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching says:
“Fix it on one point, and nothing is beyond doing.”

[Fix it on one point, and nothing is beyond doing] The Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching says: Of these five faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body), the mind is their master, and therefore you must take good charge of your own mind. The terror of a scattered mind exceeds that of a poisonous snake, a savage beast, or a murderous thief; even a raging fire is not as terrifying as it is. It is like a man holding a bowl of honey, pleased with himself, seeing only the honey in the bowl and never noticing the deep pit before him. Again, it is like a mad elephant with no iron hook to master it, galloping where it will; again, it is like a monkey that has run into the forest, leaping and springing beyond all restraint. If the mind is the least bit scattered, one must at once subdue it (draw it back), never letting it run loose. One who lets this mind run loose ruins people’s good works; one who fixes the mind on one point finds nothing beyond doing. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should strive with diligence and tame your minds. (For the original text, see in full
the Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching

) [The four foundations of mindfulness] That is: the foundation of mindfulness of body (settling mindfulness on the body), the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (settling mindfulness on feeling), the foundation of mindfulness of mind (settling mindfulness on mind), and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (settling mindfulness on phenomena). This is, through awareness and contemplation, to gather and settle mindfulness respectively on the four places — body, feeling, mind, and phenomena — making them correct rather than crooked, pure and undefiled, so that
“cultivating the state in which there is only awareness and contemplation, one transcends clinging and no longer craves or hates anything in body, mind, or world”

In this sutta the World-Honored One sets forth how to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, and how, through the foundations of mindfulness of body, of feeling, of mind, and of phenomena, to contemplate body, feeling, mind, and phenomena, thereby attaining liberation and realizing nirvāṇa.

The essential point of the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness is this: to be aware of and contemplate body, feeling, mind, and phenomena as they really are, clearly and distinctly, without clinging (without liking or disliking, taking up or putting aside). That is to say, with an equanimous mind to be aware of and contemplate body, feeling, mind, and phenomena, neither grasping nor rejecting. This is prajñā permeating ignorance; permeated long, ignorance ceases.
In awareness and contemplation, one point is extremely important: no scattering and no torpor. If the attention wanders, one must gather it back at once.
Note: For ease of understanding and reference, each passage is preceded by a number and a heading; these are not part of the sutta text.
Thus I
(Ānanda)

have heard: on one occasion the World-Honored One was dwelling among the Kurus, in the Kuru town named Kammāsadhamma, together with the Kurus. At that time the World-Honored One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” The bhikkhus answered: “World-Honored One!” The World-Honored One then gave the following teaching: “Bhikkhus! There is only one path that can purify sentient beings, overcome sorrow and lamentation, extinguish suffering and grief, practice the truth, and realize nirvāṇa — and that path is the four foundations of mindfulness.”
How precious the four foundations of mindfulness are is thus made clear!

[Ānanda] Ānanda was the Buddha’s cousin, born on the night of the Buddha’s enlightenment. Later he left home with the Buddha and served as the Buddha’s attendant, and was known for “never forgetting what had passed his ear, foremost in learning much.” When Ānanda left home, the Buddha had already taught the Dharma for twenty years, and so he asked the Buddha to repeat to him everything taught before that time; at the same time Ānanda also attained the samādhi of the self-awakening of the Dharma-nature, and could comprehend all dharmas within concentration. Therefore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Venerable Mahākāśyapa assembled the sūtra collection in the great cave of Magadha, five hundred great arhats gathered together in one place, and the assembly unanimously asked Ānanda to ascend the seat and recite the sutta texts.

Practice has two great stages. The first stage: resolving birth and death in the sense of the fragmentary, and escaping the round of rebirth; the second stage: resolving birth and death in the sense of transformation, and realizing the fruit of Buddhahood. For us beginners on the path, the urgent task is to resolve fragmentary birth and death and escape the round of rebirth. Now the root of the round of rebirth is none other than craving for body, mind, and world. Hence, when life ends, the consciousness (the self-nature) is drawn by the force of karma and takes rebirth. One who is due to enter the hells sees the mountain of knives and the forest of swords as a beautiful garden. One who is due to fall among animals takes the womb of a horse or the womb of a donkey for a splendid palace. One who keeps the precepts and does good is reborn in the human path or the heavenly path. In this sutta the World-Honored One sets forth how, through the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness, “cultivating the state in which there is only awareness and contemplation, one transcends clinging and no longer craves or hates anything in body, mind, or world,” and thus resolves fragmentary birth and death and escapes the six paths of the round of rebirth.

[Fragmentary birth and death] For sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because of the karma of good and evil that they have brought about, their life spans all have limits and their bodily forms all have divisions, and so their birth and death is called “fragmentary birth and death.” One who has resolved fragmentary birth and death is freed from the round of rebirth and escapes the three realms. [Transformational birth and death] For the noble ones who have already resolved fragmentary birth and death, in the course of cultivating the path their deluded conceptions gradually cease and their realization gradually increases; each period of this shifting between delusion and realization is different, and the passage from the earlier period into the later is just like one birth and death, and so it is called “transformational birth and death.” One who has resolved transformational birth and death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. [The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world in which beings who have the two desires of sex and food dwell, including the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below; the realm of form is the world in which beings who are free of the two desires of sex and food but still have a physical body dwell, including the four dhyānas and the eighteen heavens; the formless realm is the world in which beings who have no physical body but abide with their consciousness in deep and subtle concentration dwell, including the four heavens of emptiness (the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all the domain of the birth and death, the round of rebirth, of ordinary beings. [The six paths] Gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hells. These six are the pathways of the round of rebirth of sentient beings, and so they are called the six paths. [Transcending clinging] Having no liking or disliking, no taking up or putting aside, toward the various phenomena that arise and the various phenomena that cease in body, mind, and world.
Which four foundations of mindfulness are they?
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu
abides contemplating the body as body, ardent, aware, and mindful, having put away craving and aversion for the world;
abides contemplating feeling as feeling, ardent, aware, and mindful, having put away craving and aversion for the world;
abides contemplating mind as mind, ardent, aware, and mindful, having put away craving and aversion for the world;
abides contemplating phenomena as phenomena, ardent, aware, and mindful, having put away craving and aversion for the world.

The four foundations of mindfulness are: the foundation of mindfulness of body, of feeling, of mind, and of phenomena. This is, through ardent and aware observation of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena, to know impermanence at all times and in all places (to awaken to the fact that body, mind, and world are illusory),
so as to remove craving and aversion toward body, mind, and world

“Ardent” — this is the attitude. “Observing” and “aware” — this is the method. “Knowing impermanence at all times, removing craving and aversion toward body, mind, and world” — this is the goal. “Body,” “feeling,” “mind,” and “phenomena” — these are the objects of observation and awareness.

[Body, mind, and world are illusory] The body is a dwelling; the mind is a shadow cast by the six sense objects; the world is a dream of the round of rebirth. [The mind is a shadow cast by the six sense objects] The mind is the phantom image — deluded thoughts, discrimination, and clinging — produced when the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) come into contact with the six sense objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects). Once a person dies, the six faculties perish, and the mind is gone as well. Therefore body and mind are not you; never inject a sense of self into them (self and other, benefit and harm, gain and loss, honor and disgrace, love and hate, taking up and putting aside), or you will only seek out affliction for yourself — and still less should you let them control you. (For details, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha

Craving and aversion toward body, mind, and world — this is the root of birth and death, the round of rebirth. Remove craving and aversion toward body, mind, and world, and one cuts off birth and death, the round of rebirth, and realizes the fruit. The reason sentient beings give rise to craving and aversion toward body, mind, and world is that they falsely cling to body and mind as “I.” Yet body and mind are not you; it is the self-nature (the consciousness) within the body, which is neither born nor dies, that is you.
(For details, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha

[Knowing impermanence at all times] Impermanence is the mark of this Sahā world. For living plants and animals (humans among them), there is birth, aging, sickness, and death; for lifeless minerals, implements, and even mountains, rivers, and the great earth, there are the four marks of arising (coming into being), dwelling (maintaining), decay (deterioration), and emptiness (dispersal). To know impermanence thoroughly is to understand that whatever is born must cease,
that whatever gathers must scatter,

that everything will pass and in a blink is empty, and that resolving birth and death is the foremost matter of all. Then one will not give rise to craving for pleasant things and situations, nor to hatred for troublesome things and situations — and craving and hatred are the root of birth and death, the round of rebirth! At the same time, to know impermanence thoroughly is to warn oneself at every moment: life is short and the land is perilous and fragile; one must seize the time to practice, for when one breath does not return, one already belongs to the next life. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “Birth and death are a grave matter; impermanence comes swiftly.” The Treatise on the Perfection of Great Wisdom says: “A certain bhikkhu said: When I breathe out, I cannot be sure of breathing in again (when breathing out, one cannot be sure there will be a breath in). The Buddha said: That is called diligence, excellently cultivating the contemplation of impermanence.” [Removing craving and aversion toward body, mind, and world] Craving and aversion (love and hate, taking up and putting aside) toward body, mind, and world is the root of birth and death, the round of rebirth. Therefore, to remove craving and aversion (love and hate, taking up and putting aside) toward body, mind, and world — this is the core of practice. (See also
“Master Lianchi: A Single Stroke Erases All”

) [Craving and aversion] To crave and pursue agreeable circumstances, and to hate and resist disagreeable circumstances. Its manifestation is love and hate, taking up and putting aside. [Love and hate, taking up and putting aside] Craving, hating, pursuing, and rejecting.

blocks.text: 1. The Foundation of Mindfulness of Body

inline.s: Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu abide contemplating the body as body?

This section, “Contemplating the Breath,” and the next, “Contemplating Movements,” are the basic training for cultivating the power of awareness; they are the foundation of all the contemplations that follow, and the foundation must be laid firmly.

Awareness of the breath is a most important basic practice, and its functions are: first, to cultivate attention that is focused, continuous, and enduring; second, to tame the mind, settling the scattered mind into stillness. The mind is like a wild elephant — frenzied, restless, and enormously destructive — and so it must be tamed before its harm can be turned to benefit and it can work for us.

Awareness of the breath looks easy but is in fact rather difficult, because the attention is at any moment dragged away by deluded thoughts. The remedy, then, is: lose it, and at once recover it. That is to say, as soon as you notice that you have forgotten to be aware of the breath, immediately draw the mind back and be aware of the breath single-mindedly. Once the skill takes hold, whenever you are aware of the breath there are no deluded thoughts. With deeper skill still, when deluded thoughts fly about in profusion, you need only be single-mindedly aware of the breath and the deluded thoughts cease — this is the origin of the famous name “the sword that slays demons.” Hence it is said: When deluded thoughts rise in swarms, take the breath as your anchor.

The work of “contemplating the breath” can be done as follows: breathe abdominally, letting the breath be natural, with eyes open or closed as you please. Look inward at the abdomen, aware of and observing its rising and falling: when the abdomen rises, know clearly that the abdomen is going “up —”; when the abdomen falls, know clearly that the abdomen is going “down —.” When you first begin to practice, you may place a hand (one hand or both) on the abdomen to help you be aware of and observe its rising and falling. Once you are skilled, take the hand away and contemplate the breath. Sitting, lying down, or standing, you can contemplate the breath in this way. Once skilled, you can also contemplate the breath while walking, for example one exhalation for four steps and one inhalation for four steps. In this way, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are all spent contemplating the breath, the work is unbroken, and accomplishment comes easily.

[Abdominal breathing] On inhalation the abdomen bulges outward; on exhalation it draws inward. There are mainly two common ways of breathing: chest breathing and abdominal breathing. Chest breathing depends chiefly on the movement of the ribs and breastbone; on inhalation the chest expands front to back and side to side. Because the air goes directly into the lungs during breathing, the chest cavity expands and the abdomen stays flat. The breathing here uses the abdominal method of natural breathing, that is, on inhalation gently expanding the abdominal muscles (the abdomen bulging outward), and on exhalation gently contracting the abdominal muscles (the abdomen drawing inward). Compared with chest breathing, this way of breathing has many benefits for bodily health.

To be aware of and observe the rising and falling of the abdomen is the first step in taking up the practice. Further on, one no longer observes the rising and falling of the abdomen, but places the attention on being aware of and observing the sensations of pushing, tightening, and pressing inside the abdomen as one breathes, and these gradually go from coarse to subtle.

Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu goes into the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to a secluded and unpeopled place, sits cross-legged, straightens his body, and places his attention on the area around the mouth, keeping aware, aware of the breath as it goes out and comes in. When the in-breath is long, he clearly knows: “My in-breath is long”; when the in-breath is short, he clearly knows: “My in-breath is short”; when the out-breath is long, he clearly knows: “My out-breath is long”; when the out-breath is short, he clearly knows: “My out-breath is short.”
[Placing the attention on the area around the mouth] Placing the attention on the area between the tip of the nose and the upper lip

He trains himself thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body”; he trains himself thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body”; he trains himself thus: “I shall breathe in stilling the activity of the body”; he trains himself thus: “I shall breathe out stilling the activity of the body.”

Bhikkhus! Just as a skilled carpenter or his apprentice, when he saws a piece of wood and makes one long stroke of the saw, clearly knows: “I have made one long stroke of the saw”; and when he makes a short stroke, clearly knows: “I have made a short stroke of the saw.”

Bhikkhus! Just so, when a bhikkhu’s in-breath is long, he clearly knows: “My in-breath is long”; when the in-breath is short, he clearly knows: “My in-breath is short”; when the out-breath is long, he clearly knows: “My out-breath is long”; when the out-breath is short, he clearly knows: “My out-breath is short.”
He trains himself thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body”; he trains himself thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.”
He trains himself thus: “I shall breathe in stilling the activity of the body”; he trains himself thus: “I shall breathe out stilling the activity of the body.”
Experiencing the whole body as one breathes in, experiencing the whole body as one breathes out.
This is an exceedingly simple and effective method of practice.

Thus he abides contemplating the body internally, he abides contemplating the body externally, and he abides contemplating the body both internally and externally. He abides contemplating the phenomena of arising in the body, he abides contemplating the phenomena of ceasing in the body, and he abides contemplating the phenomena of both arising and ceasing in the body.

Thus he clearly knows: “This is the body!” Cultivating the state in which there is only awareness and contemplation, he transcends clinging and no longer craves or hates anything in body, mind, or world.
[Transcending clinging] Giving rise to no habitual reaction of craving or aversion.
[No longer craving or hating anything in body, mind, or world] This cuts off the root of birth and death, the round of rebirth, and one departs from birth and death, the round of rebirth.
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates the body as body.

This passage is spoken in terms of awareness of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down: practitioners must be clearly aware of and distinctly know each and every movement of their own, and must not fall into deluded thoughts. Therefore awareness of movements is very important — live within awareness.

There is a story of this kind. A woman went to ask the Buddha: How can I attain enlightenment? The Buddha said: What is your work? She said: I make my living by drawing water. The Buddha told her: When you draw water, you must be clearly and distinctly aware in your mind of your every movement (there must be no subconscious movement of which you are unaware). The woman earnestly did as the Buddha taught, and attained enlightenment.

Ordinary people, much if not most of the time, act subconsciously while at the same time indulging in deluded thoughts. That is to say, they move and delude themselves at once. This is a great taboo for practitioners. Therefore,
throughout the day and night, one must be aware of every movement, perform every movement consciously, and strive without slackening.

It is said that a fly came and settled on the Buddha’s face, and the Buddha gently brushed it away with his hand. Then he made the brushing movement once more. A disciple asked in wonder: “World-Honored One, the first time you brushed your hand you were driving away the fly; what was the second brushing for?” The Buddha replied: “The first was an unconscious movement, of which I was not aware, and so I made the movement a second time with awareness, to correct it.” This manifestation by the Buddha was to teach his disciples:
every movement must be clearly and distinctly known; a movement without awareness is ignorance, and one must correct it at once.
For how to be aware of movements, see
Chan of Awareness
the chapter “Awareness of Movements.”
And further, bhikkhus!
When a bhikkhu is walking, he clearly knows: “I am walking.”
When standing, he clearly knows: “I am standing.”
When sitting, he clearly knows: “I am sitting.”
When lying down, he clearly knows: “I am lying down.” Whatever his posture, he clearly knows it.

All dharmas in the world arise and cease, move and flow, and do not abide for even an instant: this is called impermanence. Impermanence is the mark of this Sahā world. For living plants and animals (humans among them), there is birth, aging, sickness, and death; for lifeless minerals, implements, and even mountains, rivers, and the great earth, there are
the four marks of arising (coming into being), dwelling (maintaining), decay (deterioration), and emptiness (dispersal)

. To know impermanence thoroughly is to understand that whatever is born must cease, whatever gathers must scatter, whatever rises must fall; that everything will pass and in a blink is empty; that resolving birth and death is the foremost matter of all; and then one will not give rise to craving for pleasant things and situations, nor to hatred for troublesome things and situations — for craving and hatred are the root of birth and death, the round of rebirth. At the same time, to know impermanence thoroughly is to warn oneself at every moment: life is short and the land is perilous and fragile; one must seize the time to practice, for when one breath does not return, one already belongs to the next life.

[The four marks of arising, dwelling, changing, and ceasing] Just as living beings have the four marks of birth, aging, sickness, and death, all things have the four marks of arising, dwelling, changing, and ceasing. The mark of arising is coming into being (conditions gather and something comes to be from nothing); the mark of dwelling is maintaining; the mark of changing is deterioration; the mark of ceasing is dispersal (conditions scatter and something passes from being into nothing). These four marks flow on without cease, this ceasing as that arises, this arising as that ceases. This is impermanence, the objective law of this world. Practitioners must have a clear understanding of this objective law. Otherwise, in the course of the four marks transforming into one another, clinging will appear in the form of love and hate, taking up and putting aside — and this is delusion and inversion. To contemplate impermanence is to awaken to impermanence at all times and in all places, so as to remove and transcend the clinging of love and hate, taking up and putting aside.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says:
“This body is impermanent, not abiding even for a thought, like a flash of lightning, a waterfall, a phantom, a mirage.”

[Like a flash of lightning, a waterfall, a phantom, a mirage] Like lightning, a waterfall, a phantom, a mirage. Lightning and a waterfall describe brevity, gone in a flash. Phantom and mirage describe what is unreal and insubstantial. “Phantom,” as when a conjurer conjures up elephants and horses. “Mirage” is the “heat haze,” the vapor produced under the blazing sun, which from afar looks like water; the thirsty deer longs to drink it and in the end can never get it. The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says:
“Just as a herd of deer, pressed by thirst, sees the haze of spring
(sees the heat haze of spring)
, and takes it for water. Deceived and confused, they rush toward it, not knowing it is not water.”
The Sutta on Impermanence says:
“There has never been a single thing that impermanence has not swallowed.”

Since everything is impermanent, what is there to delight in? What is there to crave? Therefore people since ancient times have sighed: extreme joy begets sorrow! What follows joy is sorrow, is suffering. The “Song of Deliverance” in Dream of the Red Chamber says: “All men know the immortal life is fair, but fame they cannot leave behind; where are the ministers and generals of old? A heap of wild graves, the grass grown over them. All men know the immortal life is fair, but gold and silver they cannot leave behind; to the end they only lament their hoard is small, and when at last it is large, their eyes are closed. All men know the immortal life is fair, but a pretty wife they cannot leave behind; while you live she speaks of love day after day, when you die she goes off with another man. All men know the immortal life is fair, but sons and grandsons they cannot leave behind; foolish parents there have always been in plenty, but who has ever seen a filial son
When a bhikkhu walks back and forth, he knows impermanence at every moment;
When he looks straight ahead or to the side, he knows impermanence at every moment;
When he bends his body or stretches his body, he knows impermanence at every moment;
When he puts on his robe and takes up his bowl
(bowl is written with a variant character in the text)
, he knows impermanence at every moment;
When he eats, drinks, chews, or tastes, he knows impermanence at every moment;
When he relieves himself, he knows impermanence at every moment;
When he walks, stands, sits or lies down, wakes, speaks, or is silent, he knows impermanence at every moment.

To observe and be aware of impermanence at every moment is to remove and transcend clinging to body, mind, and world: the craving and pursuit of agreeable circumstances, and the hatred and resistance toward disagreeable circumstances. Whether or not one knows impermanence thoroughly is measured by whether one still clings with love and hate, taking up and putting aside, toward body, mind, and world. To remove and transcend the clinging of love and hate, taking up and putting aside, toward body, mind, and world — this is the core of the whole sutta, and the core of practice as well!
To observe that one’s own body and the bodies of others are foul and impure. This contemplation is cultivated in order to dispel sexual desire.
And further, bhikkhus! A bhikkhu examines this body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the crown of the head downward, covered by skin and full of all kinds of impurities, thinking

In this body there are head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, lymph, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, and urine.”

It is just as if there were a grain sack with an opening at either end, filled with various kinds of grain — such as rice, brown rice, mung beans, peas, sesame, and white rice; and just as a man able to distinguish these grains, when he opens the sack, can see what is inside and tell people: “This is rice, this is brown rice, this is mung beans, this is peas, this is sesame, this is white rice.”
Bhikkhus! In the same way, a bhikkhu examines this body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the crown of the head downward, covered by skin and full of all kinds of impurities, thinking

In this body there are head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, lymph, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, and urine.”

The four great elements are the element of earth, the element of water, the element of fire, and the element of wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. All material things in the world possess these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so they are called “great.” For example: the hair, nails, teeth, skin, bones, sinews, and flesh of the human body are the element of earth, which is hard; saliva, mucus, pus, blood, phlegm, tears, and excrement and urine are the element of water, which is moist; warmth and heat are the element of fire, which is warm; and the in-breath and out-breath are the element of wind, which is moving. Again, the branches and trunk of a plant are the element of earth, which is hard; the water within its body is the element of water, which is moist; absorbing the nutrients of the soil in order to grow is the element of fire, which is warm; and taking in carbon and giving out oxygen is the element of wind, which is moving.
Contemplating the four great elements
is to contemplate: the physical body is illusory.
[Physical body] The fleshly body composed of the dharma of form, such as the four great elements.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: Sitting quietly in silence, always cherish this thought: my present body is a coming together of the four great elements — earth, fire, water, and wind. So-called head hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, and bones, marrow, brain, and filth — all belong to the element of earth; saliva, mucus, pus, blood, fluids, spittle, phlegm, tears, essence, and excrement and urine — all belong to the element of water; warmth belongs to the element of fire; movement belongs to the element of wind. If the four great elements were each to separate, where would this present body be? Thus one knows that this body has after all no permanent substance, but is a coming together of marks, truly like an illusion. (For the original text in full, see
Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment
) These words of scripture mean: the physical body is a coming together of the four great elements, and when they disperse it is no more; therefore the physical body is illusory.

When a person dies, the body rots away and nothing remains: bone and flesh return to earth, moisture returns to water, warmth returns to fire, and breath returns to wind. Where then is the body! Therefore the body is not you. The Cultivation of Mind says:
“The hundred bones
(the physical body rots)
, return to fire, return to wind
(the four great elements separate)
; one thing
(the self-nature)
long
(forever)
endures, covering heaven and earth.”

That self-nature which covers heaven and earth is you. Since the body is not you, what is there to crave in the world of body and mind that is established upon it? What is there to hate? Human life is nothing but dreaming the dream of the round of rebirth. Practice is precisely to wake from this dream.

The key to practice is, first of all, to see through the physical body and let it go. The life span of the physical body is at the shortest a few decades, at the longest about a hundred years, and it ends in death. Practitioners of course know that the physical body is a dwelling, yet because habitual tendencies work upon them, they find it hard to let go, and consciously or unconsciously always take it as “I.” Therefore one must, through study and practice, truly let it go. If one truly lets go, then even if one wanted to indulge in deluded thoughts, there would be nothing to be deluded about. For in deluded thought there is certain to be an “I,” and this “I” takes the physical body as its basis, having a name, an identity, a past, a future, and so on. Because there is this “I,” there is mine, and others, and what belongs to others, and the world in which “I” dwells. Without this “I,” the mind of itself does not move. If a deluded thought arises, one is certainly clinging to this “I” again; and if one wakes up, the deluded thought ceases — with the skin gone, what can the hair adhere to? Therefore one must practice continuously and repeatedly the work of “when a thought arises, be aware of it; once aware of it, it is gone”: when a thought arises, look at why it arose? In just what way is it clinging to “I”? Why can it not be let go? Think deeply and think it through. Do this over and over, until one truly lets go of the physical body.

Therefore, in seeing through and letting go, one must first see through and let go of the physical body (the physical body is not “I”), as when cutting down a poisonous tree, cutting straight through its root.

And further, bhikkhus! A bhikkhu examines this body, whatever its place or posture, in terms of the characteristics of the elements that compose it, contemplating thus: “The element of earth, the element of water, the element of fire, and the element of wind — this is the body!”
Bhikkhus! It is just as when a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice kills a cow and cuts it up into pieces, and then they sit at a crossroads.

The meaning is: it is just like a butcher or a butcher’s apprentice who kills a cow, cuts it into pieces, and lays them out at a crossroads to sell. Passers-by each buy a piece and carry it away — where is the cow then? This illustrates how after death the corpse rots, the four great elements separate, and where is the body then? Thus the body is not “I,” and one transcends clinging to the body (the belief that the body is “I”).

Bhikkhus! In the same way, a bhikkhu examines this body, whatever its place or posture, in terms of the elements that compose it, contemplating thus: “The element of earth, the element of water, the element of fire, and the element of wind — this is the body!”

Enter deeply into this contemplation: your fleshly body is dying, and then comes the end of the mind (feelings, thoughts, and emotions), and the world passes away with it. Yet you — the self-nature — are still there. If the self-nature is awakened, one then attains liberation, transcends birth and death, and forever enjoys the bliss of the Dharma; if the self-nature is still deluded, then, drawn along by the karma one has created, one goes on being born and dying in the six paths, in the round of rebirth.
[The six paths] Gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hells.

It has long been the custom of our people to avoid speaking of death, thinking that once the body dies there is nothing left at all. And so at the very mention of death a chill and horror rise of themselves. In truth the body is only the dwelling of the self-nature; dwellings arise and decay, while the self-nature endures. To contemplate the cemetery is precisely to awaken to the fact that the body is not you, and therefore to stop craving and clinging to it. By contemplating the various states of the body after death, one comes to turn away from one’s own body and the bodies of others, and removes craving and clinging toward body, mind, and world.

As for death, everyone knows that they will die, and yet in the subconscious it is often otherwise. In the subconscious people usually hold one of the following views and stances: first, “I will not die”; second, “I will die — so let me drink today while there is wine, and worry tomorrow about tomorrow’s sorrow, and simply muddle along”; third, “I will die, everyone will die, and there is no help for it, so I may as well enjoy myself as much as I can”; fourth, “I will die, but I can be liberated in death, never again to undergo the sufferings of birth, aging, sickness, and death, but to be peaceful, joyful, and free.” These latent views and stances guide and even control people’s thinking and behavior.

Note carefully: the views and stances spoken of here are the views and stances that actually guide and control your thinking and behavior, not the views and stances you suppose yourself to hold. For example, in principle everyone knows that whatever is born must die, and one may even expound on it to others. But amid circumstances and conditions one’s actual thinking and behavior are otherwise — as in the line “To the end he only laments his hoard is small; when at last it is large, his eyes are closed,” which describes exactly this situation.

Practitioners must first establish a correct view and stance with regard to death: “I will die, but I can be liberated in death, never again to undergo the sufferings of birth, aging, sickness, and death, but to be peaceful, joyful, and free.” And amid circumstances and conditions they must temper themselves unceasingly, so that this view and stance become ever firmer and ever more deeply carried out in every word and action, in every thought and every moment. In what follows, through the insight of contemplating a corpse, one rouses oneself: one must stand firm in the correct view and stance, let go of all conditions, and strive in practice.

And further, bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu in the cemetery sees a corpse thrown aside, one day, two days, or three days dead, swollen, discolored, and festering, he thinks of his own body thus: “Truly, my body too is of this nature, will become like this, and cannot escape such an outcome.”

And further, bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu in the cemetery sees a corpse thrown aside, pecked at by crows, vultures, hawks, and herons, or gnawed by wild dogs, tigers, leopards, and jackals, or eaten by various other kinds of living beings, he thinks of his own body thus: “Truly, my body too is of this nature, will become like this, and cannot escape such an outcome.”

And further, bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu in the cemetery sees a corpse thrown aside, with only a skeleton left, some flesh and blood still clinging to the bones and sinews binding the bones together, he thinks of his own body thus: “Truly, my body too is of this nature, will become like this, and cannot escape such an outcome.”

And further, bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu in the cemetery sees a corpse thrown aside, with only blood-smeared bones left, without skin or flesh, and the sinews binding the bones together, he thinks of his own body thus: “Truly, my body too is of this nature, will become like this, and cannot escape such an outcome.”

And further, bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu in the cemetery sees a corpse thrown aside, with only bones left, flesh and blood quite gone, and the sinews binding the bones together, he thinks of his own body thus: “Truly, my body too is of this nature, will become like this, and cannot escape such an outcome.”

And further, bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu in the cemetery sees a corpse thrown aside, with only a heap of bones scattered in every direction — here a hand bone, there a foot bone; here an ankle bone, there a knee bone; here a thigh bone, there a hip bone; this a spine, that a shoulder blade; and further shoulder bones, neck bones, jawbones, teeth, and skull — he thinks of his own body thus: “Truly, my body too is of this nature, will become like this, and cannot escape such an outcome.”

And further, bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu in the cemetery sees a corpse thrown aside, with only a heap of bones whitened like conch shells, he thinks of his own body thus: “Truly, my body too is of this nature, will become like this, and cannot escape such an outcome.”

And further, bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu in the cemetery sees a corpse thrown aside, with the bones piled in a heap after more than a year, he thinks of his own body thus: “Truly, my body too is of this nature, will become like this, and cannot escape such an outcome.”

Thus he clearly knows: “This is the body!” Cultivating the state in which there is only awareness and contemplation, he transcends clinging and no longer craves or hates anything in body, mind, or world. Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates the body as body.

And further, bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu in the cemetery sees a corpse thrown aside, with the bones rotted to powder, he thinks of his own body thus: “Truly, my body too is of this nature, will become like this, and cannot escape such an outcome.”

blocks.text: 2. The Foundation of Mindfulness of Feeling

inline.s: When the six faculties come into contact with the six sense objects, feelings arise; one must at every moment be perfectly clear about one’s present feelings.

[The six faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The eye is the faculty of seeing, the ear the faculty of hearing, the nose the faculty of smelling, the tongue the faculty of tasting, the body the faculty of touching, and the mind the faculty of thinking. [The six sense objects] The object of form, the object of sound, the object of smell, the object of taste, the object of touch, and the object of mental phenomena. An object means that which defiles; it is said to be able to defile people’s pure minds, so that the true nature cannot manifest. They are also called the six conditions, that is, the conditions taken as objects by the six faculties. [The object of mental phenomena] The karmic seeds stored in the ālayavijñāna. (For details, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
the section “The Working Process of the Consciousness-Mind.”)
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate feeling as feeling?
contemplating feeling
To observe feelings, and thereby transcend clinging to feelings. [Clinging] To inject a sense of self into something, grasp it and not let go, and be unable to transcend it.
Bhikkhus!

When experiencing a pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: “I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.” When experiencing a painful feeling, he clearly knows: “I am experiencing a painful feeling.” When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: “I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

When he clings to a pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: “I am clinging to a pleasant feeling.” When he does not cling to a pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: “I am not clinging to a pleasant feeling.”
When clinging to a painful feeling, he clearly knows: “I am clinging to a painful feeling.” When not clinging to a painful feeling, he clearly knows: “I am not clinging to a painful feeling.”
Question: One may speak of clinging to pleasure, but when in pain one wishes it would hurry away — how can one speak of clinging to pain?

Answer: Body and mind are both illusory (see the note to the next chapter, “The Foundation of Mindfulness of Mind”), and therefore feelings too are illusory. In fact many sufferings are not physical sufferings but mental sufferings. Physical suffering can be resolved by medical treatment. Mental suffering, however, must be cured by the medicine of the mind. Mental suffering has its root in your injecting a sense of self into a certain situation and resisting the arising of that situation — this is clinging. The stronger the sense of self injected, the fiercer the resistance; that is, the greater the clinging, the greater and more enduring the suffering. If you draw the sense of self out of the situation and accept it without resistance, simply observing in stillness the feelings it gives rise to, the suffering will gradually lessen until it disappears — and this depends on the degree to which you transcend clinging.
As for physical suffering, one may contemplate pain in this way:

For a beginner, after sitting in meditation for about half an hour or forty-five minutes, you will find that your limbs begin to ache dully, or that you feel stabbing pains and other discomforts. When such sensations arise, this is a good opportunity to contemplate “the feeling of suffering,” to penetrate the true nature of pain so as to see its arising and ceasing. For the specific method of contemplation, see
Mindfulness Meditation
the section “The Technique and Process of Contemplating Pain.”

When clinging to a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: “I am clinging to a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.” When not clinging to a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he clearly knows: “I am not clinging to a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

Thus he dwells contemplating feeling as feeling internally, he dwells contemplating feeling as feeling externally, and he dwells contemplating feeling as feeling both internally and externally. Therefore he dwells contemplating the arising of feelings, he dwells contemplating the passing away of feelings, and he dwells contemplating feelings both arising and passing away.
Then he clearly knows: ‘This is feeling!’ Having cultivated a state of mere knowing and reflection, he transcends clinging and no longer craves or is averse to anything in body, mind, or the world.
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates feeling as feeling.
The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

‘All sentient beings, from time without beginning, give rise to all kinds of inversion, like a deluded person who loses his bearings and mistakes one direction for another, falsely taking the four great elements as the marks of his own body and the shadows of the six sense objects as the marks of his own mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in space and a second moon.’

(Translation: All sentient beings, from time without beginning, are deluded as to their own true nature and give rise to all kinds of inversion, taking the false as real. It is like a person who has lost his bearings and takes north for south, east for west, falsely taking the fleshly body formed of the four great elements — earth, water, fire, and wind — as the marks of his own body, and the deliberating mind that arises when the six faculties come into contact with the six sense objects (the shadows of the six sense objects) as the marks of his own mind. It is like a person whose eyes are diseased, who deludedly sees flowers in space and a second moon.)

[The four great elements] All tangible matter in the world is composed of the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, and is therefore called ‘great’: the great element of earth, the great element of water, the great element of fire, and the great element of wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. [The shadows of the six sense objects] The mind is what arises when the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) come into contact with the six sense objects (form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mind-objects), producing deluded thoughts, discrimination, and clinging; hence it is called the shadows of the six sense objects — the illusory shadows that appear when the six faculties come into contact with the six sense objects. [Flowers in space] That is, flowers in the sky. ‘Flower’ is an ancient variant of ‘flower.’

This is to say that body and mind are both illusions, yet sentient beings deludedly cling to them as real. It is like a person whose eyes are diseased, who deludedly sees flowers in space (though there never were any flowers in space) and a second moon. To contemplate the mind is to see this mind clearly and to realize that the mind is a product of the six faculties coming into contact with the six sense objects: when the body dies, the six faculties perish, and the mind is gone as well. Therefore body and mind are not you; never inject a sense of self into them, or you will only bring trouble upon yourself — still less should you let them take control of you.
And further, bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate mind as mind?
contemplating the mind
To contemplate the mind is to see how the mind is controlling you, and thereby to free yourself from its control.
When the mind has craving, he clearly knows that the mind has craving; when the mind is free of craving, he clearly knows that the mind is free of craving.
When the mind has hatred, he clearly knows that the mind has hatred; when the mind is free of hatred, he clearly knows that the mind is free of hatred.
When the mind has delusion, he clearly knows that the mind has delusion; when the mind is free of delusion, he clearly knows that the mind is free of delusion.
When the mind is collected, he clearly knows that the mind is collected; when the mind is scattered, he clearly knows that the mind is scattered.
When the mind is expansive, he clearly knows that the mind is expansive; when the mind is narrow, he clearly knows that the mind is narrow.
[The expansive mind] The mind is vast in measure, with no sense of self or other, right or wrong.
When the mind is
elated
(a positive state of mind), he clearly knows that the mind is
elated
; when the mind is
depressed
(a negative state of mind), he clearly knows that the mind is depressed
When the mind is concentrated, he clearly knows that the mind is concentrated; when the mind is not concentrated, he clearly knows that the mind is not concentrated.
When the mind is liberated, he clearly knows that the mind is liberated; when the mind is not liberated, he clearly knows that the mind is not liberated.
[A liberated mind] Free of deluded thoughts, pure and at ease, unentangled by any object or condition.

Thus he dwells contemplating mind as mind internally, he dwells contemplating mind as mind externally, and he dwells contemplating mind as mind both internally and externally. Therefore he dwells contemplating the arising of mind states, he dwells contemplating the passing away of mind states, and he dwells contemplating mind states both arising and passing away.
[The internal mind] The mind that clings to internal objects. [The external mind] The mind that clings to external objects.
Then he clearly knows: ‘This is mind!’ Having cultivated a state of mere knowing and reflection, he transcends clinging and no longer craves or is averse to anything in body, mind, or the world.
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates mind as mind.
[Contemplation of dharmas] To settle the thoughts upon the Dharma of the path, so that they are right and not wrong.
Contemplating the five hindrances means extinguishing these five afflictions through observing the five hindrances.

[The five hindrances] Five kinds of affliction. ‘Hindrance’ is another name for affliction, because afflictions can cover over people’s mind-nature and prevent wholesome dharmas from arising. The five hindrances are: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt about the Dharma.
sloth and torpor
The torpor and drowsiness that arise during meditation.

[Restlessness and remorse] Restlessness (the mind wavering) and remorse. Both of these mental states rob the mind of peace and give rise to affliction. [Doubt about the Dharma] Doubting that the Dharma of the path is the true path, and therefore holding it in no respect, with no faith, no acceptance, and no practice.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate dharmas as dharmas?
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu contemplates dharmas as dharmas, that is, he contemplates dharmas as dharmas in terms of the five hindrances.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate dharmas as dharmas, that is, how does he contemplate dharmas as dharmas in terms of the five hindrances?

When a bhikkhu gives rise to sensual desire, he clearly knows: ‘I have given rise to sensual desire’; when a bhikkhu does not give rise to sensual desire, he clearly knows: ‘I have not given rise to sensual desire.’ He clearly knows that unarisen sensual desire has arisen; he clearly knows that sensual desire now arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that sensual desire now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

When a bhikkhu gives rise to ill will, he clearly knows: ‘I have given rise to ill will’; when a bhikkhu does not give rise to ill will, he clearly knows: ‘I have not given rise to ill will.’ He clearly knows that unarisen ill will has arisen; he clearly knows that ill will now arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that ill will now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

When a bhikkhu gives rise to sloth and torpor, he clearly knows: ‘I have given rise to sloth and torpor’; when a bhikkhu does not give rise to sloth and torpor, he clearly knows: ‘I have not given rise to sloth and torpor.’ He clearly knows that unarisen sloth and torpor have arisen; he clearly knows that sloth and torpor now arisen have been abandoned; he clearly knows that sloth and torpor now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

When a bhikkhu gives rise to restlessness and remorse, he clearly knows: ‘I have given rise to restlessness and remorse’; when a bhikkhu does not give rise to restlessness and remorse, he clearly knows: ‘I have not given rise to restlessness and remorse.’ He clearly knows that unarisen restlessness and remorse have arisen; he clearly knows that restlessness and remorse now arisen have been abandoned; he clearly knows that restlessness and remorse now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

When a bhikkhu gives rise to doubt about the Dharma, he clearly knows: ‘I have given rise to doubt’; when a bhikkhu does not give rise to doubt, he clearly knows: ‘I have not given rise to doubt.’ He clearly knows that unarisen doubt has arisen; he clearly knows that doubt now arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that doubt now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

Thus he dwells contemplating dharmas as dharmas internally, he dwells contemplating dharmas as dharmas externally, and he dwells contemplating dharmas as dharmas both internally and externally. Therefore he dwells contemplating the arising of dharmas, he dwells contemplating the passing away of dharmas, and he dwells contemplating dharmas both arising and passing away.
Then he clearly knows: ‘These are dharmas!’ Having cultivated a state of mere knowing and reflection, he transcends clinging and no longer craves or is averse to anything in body, mind, or the world.
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates dharmas as dharmas, that is, he contemplates dharmas as dharmas in terms of the five hindrances.
Contemplating the five aggregates means observing the arising and ceasing of the workings of body, mind, and world, so that delusion and falsity do not hold power.

[The five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. These five are produced by heaping up and gathering together, and so are called the ‘five aggregates’; they can also cover over people’s true nature, causing them to be deluded and inverted and to create all kinds of karma, and so they are also named the ‘five coverings.’ Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called ‘form-dharmas’; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness belong to the mental and are called ‘mind-dharmas.’ These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Among them, the aggregate of form is the body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness) are the mind.

The workings of the mind come about through the cooperative operation of the eight consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, manas consciousness, and ālayavijñāna). The process is: feeling → perception → mental formations → consciousness. ‘Feeling’ is the reception that occurs when the faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) come into contact with objects (form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mind-objects). ‘Perception’ is the thinking (analyzing, judging, and synthesizing) that arises in dependence upon feeling, and the basis for its analysis and judgment is constantly drawn from the eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and supplied by the seventh consciousness (manas). ‘Mental formations’ are the mental activities (the mind’s inner workings) that arise in dependence upon that thinking — for example, love and hate, likes and dislikes, grasping and rejecting, and the issuing of instructions for action to body and speech; this is the creation of karma. ‘Consciousness’ gathers all the information from the three preceding links of feeling, perception, and mental formations into a comprehensive discernment — the karmic consciousness — which is then fed through the seventh consciousness into the eighth consciousness and stored away for later use; these are what are called karmic seeds.

[Karmic seeds] The karma created by sentient beings is stored in the ālayavijñāna, and because it can produce manifest activity, flower, and bear fruit, it is called a seed. Karmic seeds are also called karmic habitual tendencies, or simply seeds or habitual tendencies; they exert a latent influence — even control — over people’s thoughts and behavior.

In the workings of the mind, the link of ‘perception’ can be controlled deliberately. Practitioners use the ‘perception’ of wisdom to bring about right ‘mental formations,’ thereby weakening and eliminating habitual tendencies. The key to turning circumstances by the mind lies precisely in working at the link of ‘perception,’ which is what is meant by turning the thought. For example, when ordinary people hear themselves slandered they grow angry, yet in the Liaofan’s Four Lessons Mr. Liaofan’s skill at turning the thought was this: he reflected, ‘In all the world there is no hero who takes himself to be always right, and no learning that lays the blame on others. When a matter is not accomplished, it is always because my own virtue is not well cultivated, so that I cannot move others to support me and join me in bringing it to completion with one heart. Whenever I meet with adversity, I seek the cause entirely within myself. In this way, all slander becomes a fine opportunity to temper me, uplift me, and bring me to accomplishment. I have not even time to be grateful — how could I be angry? Moreover, when I am slandered and attacked by others, if only I do not grow angry, then even if their fury blazes to the heavens, it is no more than raising a fire to burn the sky. With nothing to burn, the fire goes out of itself. But if I am slandered and attacked and I grow angry and enraged, then though I argue with all my cleverness, I am only spinning a cocoon around myself and bringing on endless trouble. So anger is not only useless but harmful.’ (For the original text, see
The Annotated Liaofan’s Four Lessons

.) And so he not only did not grow angry but gladly accepted it, correcting his faults if he had them and encouraging himself if he did not. In this way he not only weakened but even uprooted the karmic seeds of past anger at slander — this is the way to eliminate habitual tendencies.

You must examine yourself at all times and in all places: are you being controlled by ignorance? Have you fallen into a habitual pattern of thinking (a habitual reaction)? If so, step out of it at once and let wisdom take charge. In fact, resistance, discontent, criticism, anxiety, irritation, and waiting are, for practitioners, all manifestations of ignorance; they are tigers blocking the road to bodhi, and they are also reminders that you have fallen into ignorance once again.

Modern psychology has an ABC theory: A stands for the Activating event, B stands for Belief — the interpretation of the activating event, and C stands for Consequence — the emotional and behavioral outcome. People always hope for a good A (event) and avoid a bad A, and they strive unceasingly to that end. Yet they do not know that B (interpretation) is the one factor you can fully control and change, and that what brings about C (consequence) is not A but B. This B (interpretation) is precisely the link of ‘perception’ among feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The same event brings joy to some households and sorrow to others. Why? Because their interpretations of the event differ (their thoughts differ)! Therefore the sage turns the mind and does not turn circumstances, while the ordinary person turns circumstances and does not turn the mind. So we need the wisdom of taking one step back to reflect and of turning the thought to reflect, making the present conditions serve us. For example, suppose you are assigned the task of sweeping the floor. One thought is: why should I be sent to do such a trivial chore? — and you feel aggrieved. Turn the thought around: sweeping the floor is sweeping the mind; this is a wonderful opportunity to test the mind amid circumstances — and you accept it gladly. In the process of sweeping, from the matter to the principle, you sweep away the rubbish outside and the afflictions within, and so sweeping the floor becomes a wonderful opportunity to grind away self-conceit and cultivate concentration in the midst of movement.

The foregoing explains the ‘perception (thought)’ of wisdom, which brings about right ‘mental formations (the mind’s activity)’; hence one should constantly contemplate with wisdom. Of course, if one can eliminate perception altogether, that is even more sharp and direct — like felling a poisonous tree by cutting straight through its root. For all sentient beings are deluded as to their own original mind and have always acted wholly on deluded thought; therefore in cultivation now, the elimination of perception is foremost.

To change one’s own destiny, and even to eliminate habitual tendencies and be free of birth and death, the key is to make the mind able to turn karma. The mind can create karma, and it can also turn karma. Karma is created by the mind and also turns with the mind. If the mind cannot turn karma, then it is bound by karma; if karma does not turn with the mind, then it can bind the mind. How can the mind turn karma? When the mind is united with the Way, it can turn karma. How can karma bind the mind? When the mind follows habitual tendencies and lets things run their course in receiving and reacting, it is bound by karma. All present circumstances and all future karmic retributions are only what karma has brought about and only what the mind manifests. Because they are only what karma has brought about, the retribution that comes from former circumstances is entirely fixed — this is because karma can bind the mind. Because they are only what the mind manifests, the retribution that comes from former circumstances is entirely unfixed — this is because the mind can turn karma. If, just when karma is able to bind the mind and the retribution from former circumstances is fixed, one suddenly brings forth the bodhi mind and cultivates true practice, uniting the mind with the Way, then the mind can turn karma, and the retribution from former circumstances, though fixed, becomes unfixed. But if, just when the mind is able to turn karma and the retribution from former circumstances is unfixed, the bodhi mind suddenly retreats and true practice falls short, then karma can bind the mind, and the retribution from former circumstances, though unfixed, becomes fixed. Karma, however, was created in the past, and there is no helping that; but fortunately, whether or not one brings forth the aspiration lies within one’s own power. Creating karma and turning karma do not depend on others.
Therefore, practitioners should, in accordance with conditions, let their old karma dissolve and refrain from creating new misfortunes.
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the five aggregates subject to clinging.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena, that is, how does he contemplate phenomena in terms of the five aggregates subject to clinging?
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu clearly knows:
‘This is form; this is the arising of form; this is the ceasing of form;
‘This is feeling; this is the arising of feeling; this is the ceasing of feeling;
‘This is perception; this is the arising of perception; this is the ceasing of perception;
‘These are mental formations; this is the arising of mental formations; this is the ceasing of mental formations;
‘This is consciousness; this is the arising of consciousness; this is the ceasing of consciousness.’
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the five aggregates subject to clinging.

blocks.text: 3. Contemplating the Sense Faculties and Sense Objects

inline.s: Contemplating the six sense faculties and the six sense objects, in order to awaken to the source of bondage.

[The six sense faculties] are the six internal bases: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The eye is the faculty of seeing, the ear of hearing, the nose of smelling, the tongue of tasting, the body of touching, and the mind of thinking. A root means that from which things grow — just as a plant with roots puts forth branches and trunks, so consciousness arises dependent upon conditions, and with the six faculties the six consciousnesses arise, in the same way. [The six sense objects] are the six external bases: form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects. An object means that which defiles; it can defile the pure minds of people and prevent true nature from manifesting. They are also called the six realms, that is, the external objects to which the six faculties are directed. [The six consciousnesses] are eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. These are the discriminating functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and thinking that arise when the six faculties meet the six objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects.
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the six internal bases and the six external bases.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena, that is, how does he contemplate phenomena in terms of the six internal bases and the six external bases?

Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu clearly knows the eye faculty, clearly knows forms, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the ear faculty, clearly knows sounds, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the nose faculty, clearly knows smells, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the tongue faculty, clearly knows tastes, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the body faculty, clearly knows tangibles, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the mind faculty, clearly knows mental objects, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.
[The mind faculty] The seventh of the eight consciousnesses, the manas consciousness, is the mind faculty.

[The eight consciousnesses] ālayavijñāna, manas-vijñāna, mano-vijñāna, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness. Among these, the ālayavijñāna is the fundamental consciousness; the other seven consciousnesses are all derived from it. [The mental object] That which the mind faculty takes as its object (the karmic seeds) is called the mental object.
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the six internal bases and the six external bases.

blocks.text: 4. Contemplating the Seven Factors of Enlightenment

inline.s: The Amitabha Buddha Sūtra says:

‘In that land there are always many kinds of wonderful and richly colored birds: white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śarīs, kalaviṅkas, and two-hearted birds. These many birds, through the six periods of day and night, sing forth harmonious and beautiful sounds. Their songs proclaim the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eight factors of the noble path, and teachings such as these.’
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
‘The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the bodhisattva’s Pure Land.’
From this we can see the importance of cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment.
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment

the four establishments of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path (that is, the eight factors of the noble path). [The four establishments of mindfulness] First, contemplation of the body; second, contemplation of feeling; third, contemplation of mind; fourth, contemplation of phenomena. [The four right efforts] ‘Right effort’ means the ability to practice with great diligence: abandon evil that has already arisen, prevent evil that has not yet arisen, give rise to good that has not yet arisen, and increase the good that has already arisen. Practicing these four aspects of the path with vigor, urging on body, speech, and mind, to cut off evil and cultivate good. [The four bases of psychic power] Also called the four roads to psychic power; by cultivating these four one can realize supernormal powers at will. First, the base of psychic power of desire — the increase of the aspiration to cultivate the path and attain its fruit; second, the base of psychic power of mind — single-minded thought, abiding in right principle; third, the base of psychic power of energy — vigorous advance with no break in the work; fourth, the base of psychic power of wisdom — true illumination free from delusion, the mind no longer distracted.

[The five faculties] The faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. These five are the roots from which the noble path is born, hence they are called the ‘five faculties.’ [The five powers] The strength produced when the five faculties are firmly established is called the ‘five powers’: faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The power of faith is the growth of the faculty of faith, which destroys all wrong belief; the power of energy is the growth of the faculty of energy, which destroys the body’s sloth; the power of mindfulness is the growth of the faculty of mindfulness, which destroys all wrong thoughts; the power of concentration is the growth of the faculty of concentration, which destroys all scattered thinking; the power of wisdom is the growth of the faculty of wisdom, which destroys all the delusions of the three realms.
[Bodhi] Rendered into Chinese as ‘awakening,’ it is the great wisdom that cuts off afflictions. [The seven factors of enlightenment]

The seven kinds of awakening revealed through the five faculties and five powers. First, the factor of mindfulness — at all times reflecting on the true Dharma, keeping concentration and wisdom in balance; second, the factor of dharma-investigation — using wisdom to examine the true and the false of phenomena; third, the factor of energy — practicing the true Dharma with courageous vigor; fourth, the factor of joy — the mind, obtaining the good Dharma, gives rise to gladness; fifth, the factor of tranquillity — removing the gross afflictions of body and mind so as to attain ease and peace; sixth, the factor of concentration — the mind resting on a single object, no longer scattering; seventh, the factor of equanimity — letting go of all delusive phenomena and earnestly practicing the true Dharma.

[The eightfold path] The eightfold practice of the noble ones. First, right view, that is, correct understanding; second, right intention, that is, correct thinking; third, right speech, that is, proper speech; fourth, right action, that is, proper conduct; fifth, right livelihood, that is, a proper occupation or way of life; sixth, right effort, that is, proper striving; seventh, right mindfulness, that is, correct attention; eighth, right concentration, that is, correct concentration. By cultivating this eightfold path one can realize the fruit of arhatship.
And further, bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena?
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena, that is, how does he contemplate phenomena in terms of the seven factors of enlightenment?

Bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of mindfulness’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of mindfulness, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of mindfulness.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of mindfulness has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of mindfulness has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of dharma-investigation, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of dharma-investigation’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of dharma-investigation, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of dharma-investigation.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of dharma-investigation has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of dharma-investigation has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of energy, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of energy’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of energy, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of energy.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of energy has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of energy has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of joy, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of joy’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of joy, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of joy.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of joy has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of joy has reached full development.
