When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of tranquillity, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of tranquillity’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of tranquillity, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of tranquillity.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of tranquillity has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of tranquillity has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of concentration, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of concentration’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of concentration, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of concentration.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of concentration has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of concentration has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of equanimity’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of equanimity, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of equanimity.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of equanimity has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of equanimity has reached full development.

Then he clearly realizes: ‘This is the Dharma!’ Having cultivated a state of mere knowing and reflection, he transcends clinging and no longer craves or is averse to anything in body, mind, or the world.
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Craving is the root of the various sufferings, such as birth and death. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
‘All sentient beings, from time without beginning, because of manifold affections and craving, are caught up in the round of rebirth;
Know that the round of rebirth is rooted in love.
Therefore, sentient beings who wish to escape birth and death and free themselves from the round of rebirth should first cut off craving and remove the thirst of love.’
And the Four Noble Truths are the essential path that extinguishes craving and delivers one from all the suffering of birth and death.

The Four Noble Truths are: the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path. The origin is the cause of suffering, and suffering is the result of the origin; the path is the cause of cessation, and cessation is the result of the path.

That is to say: the various sufferings of birth and death (suffering) are gathered together by craving (origin); and to extinguish craving (cessation), one can only cultivate the noble path (path). The Buddha said:
‘This is suffering, and you should understand it; this is the origin, and you should abandon it; this is the path, and you should cultivate it; this is cessation, and you should realize it.’
Therefore,
practitioners should be diligent and earnest, knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, cultivating the path, and realizing cessation

[Truth] The principle that is real and without error. [The Four Noble Truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of its origin, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path. First, the ‘truth of suffering’ sets forth the truth that life is filled with suffering. Suffering has the character of oppression. Life involves the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and innumerable sufferings; suffering is the truth of actual human life. Second, ‘origin’ in the ‘truth of the origin of suffering’ means to gather and bring about; it sets forth the truth of how the suffering of life arises. The suffering of life is due to craving, and then to clinging, then to karma, then to suffering, then to rebirth. Third, the ‘truth of cessation’ sets forth the truth of extinguishing all suffering. When the whole origin of suffering (craving) is cut off forever without remainder, with no grasping and no clinging, one no longer creates karma, suffers, or is reborn; this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the ‘truth of the path’ sets forth the truth of how forever to cut off the origin of suffering (craving), that is, the path to the extinction of suffering — the eightfold noble path. Among the Four Noble Truths, the origin is the cause and suffering is the result; the path is the cause and cessation is the result.

[The three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned states. The suffering of suffering: worldly beings have a body subject to birth and death, which is already suffering enough, and with all kinds of suffering pressing upon them, it is suffering piled upon suffering, hence it is called the suffering of suffering; the suffering of change is the suffering felt when an occasional pleasant state is lost; the suffering of conditioned states is the suffering of all conditioned things being impermanent and ceaselessly flowing, never at rest. [The eight sufferings] First, the suffering of birth, the pain at the time of birth; second, the suffering of aging, the pain of old age and bodily weakness; third, the suffering of sickness, the pain of illness; fourth, the suffering of death, the pain at the time of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from the loved, the pain of parting with those one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting with the hated, the pain of associating with those one hates; seventh, the suffering of not getting what one seeks, the pain of unfulfilled desires; eighth, the suffering of the raging of the five aggregates, the suffering in which the activity of the five aggregates (the five aggregates) blazes and covers over true nature. [The eightfold noble path] Also called the eightfold path, the eightfold practice of the noble ones: first, right view, correct understanding; second, right intention, correct thinking; third, right speech, proper speech; fourth, right action, proper conduct; fifth, right livelihood, a proper occupation and way of life; sixth, right effort, correct striving; seventh, right mindfulness, correct attention; eighth, right concentration, correct concentration. By cultivating this eightfold noble path one can realize the fruit of arhatship.
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the Four Noble Truths.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena, that is, how does he contemplate phenomena in terms of the Four Noble Truths?

Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu clearly knows as it really is: this is suffering. He clearly knows as it really is: this is the origin of suffering. He clearly knows as it really is: this is the cessation of suffering. He clearly knows as it really is: this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the hated is suffering; separation from the loved is suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering. In short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.

[The five aggregates subject to clinging] Clinging means grasping and clinging; an aggregate means accumulation; the aggregates arise from clinging, hence they are called aggregates subject to clinging. The five aggregates subject to clinging: first, the aggregate of form subject to clinging; second, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging; third, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging; fourth, the aggregate of mental formations subject to clinging; fifth, the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.

And what, bhikkhus, is birth? For whatever beings, in whatever class of beings, there is the taking of rebirth, descent, arising, the emergence of the aggregates, and the obtaining of the internal and external bases — this, bhikkhus, is called birth.

And what, bhikkhus, is aging? For whatever beings, in whatever class of beings, there is the decay, decrepitude, the falling out of teeth, the greying of hair, the wrinkling of skin, the nearing of the end of life, and the exhaustion of the faculties — this, bhikkhus, is aging.

And what, bhikkhus, is death? For whatever beings, in whatever class of beings, there is the falling away, passing away, breaking up, disappearance, the ending of the life span, the dissolution of the aggregates, the abandoning of the body, and the cutting off of life — this, bhikkhus, is death.

And what, bhikkhus, is sorrow? Whenever anyone, at any time, affected by loss or misfortune, gives rise to these painful states of mind — sorrowing, mourning, grieving, deep grief, and profound lamentation — this, bhikkhus, is sorrow.

And what, bhikkhus, is lamentation? Whenever anyone, at any time, affected by loss or misfortune, gives rise to weeping, wailing, lamenting, and the state of wailing and lamenting — this, bhikkhus, is lamentation.
And what, bhikkhus, is pain? Bhikkhus! Whatever bodily pain, discomfort, or unpleasant feeling arises from bodily contact — this, bhikkhus, is pain.
And what, bhikkhus, is grief? Bhikkhus
— whatever mental pain, discomfort, or any painful, unpleasant feeling that arises from mental contact — this, bhikkhus, is grief.

And what, bhikkhus, is despair? Whenever anyone, at any time, affected by loss or misfortune, gives rise to these states of mind — agitation, distress, sorrowful agitation, and vexation — this, bhikkhus, is despair.

And what, bhikkhus, is the suffering of association with the hated? Whenever anyone, at any time or place, encounters unpleasant, disliked forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, or at all times and places meets with misfortune, harm, hardship, or distress, and there is meeting, association, contact, or union with them — this, bhikkhus, is called the suffering of association with the hated.

And what, bhikkhus, is the suffering of separation from the loved? Whenever anyone, at any time or place, is separated from the agreeable, pleasing, beloved sense objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; when people who wish him well and hope for his fortune, prosperity, comfort, or safety — such as parents, brothers and sisters, friends, colleagues, and relatives — are separated from him, so that he cannot see, approach, or associate with them — this, bhikkhus, is called the suffering of separation from the loved.

And what, bhikkhus, is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings who are subject to birth give rise to this wish: ‘May we not be subject to birth! May we not be reborn again!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.
Bhikkhus! What is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings subject to aging give rise to this wish
‘May we not be subject to aging! May we not be subject to aging!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.
Bhikkhus! What is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings subject to illness give rise to this wish
‘May we not be subject to illness! May we be free of illness!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.
Bhikkhus! What is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings subject to death give rise to this wish
‘May we not be subject to death! May we never die!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.
Bhikkhus! What is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair give rise to this wish

‘May we not be subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair! May we no longer sorrow, lament, suffer pain, grieve, or despair!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.

Bhikkhus! What is meant by ‘in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering’? The aggregate of form subject to clinging is suffering, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging is suffering, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging is suffering, the aggregate of mental formations subject to clinging is suffering, the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging is suffering. Bhikkhus! This is what is meant by ‘in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.’
Bhikkhus! This is the noble truth of suffering.

Craving is the origin of suffering (craving brings about suffering) and is the root of suffering. Because of craving there is clinging; because of clinging, karma; because of karma, suffering; because of suffering, rebirth. Craving arises at the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind) meeting the six sense objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, mental object); therefore one must guard the gates of the six faculties, and upon contact with the sense objects, shine the light of awareness and cut off the root of delusion — this is the key.
And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

It is craving, the craving that brings about continued rebirth, that is bound up with delight and lust, and that seeks delight here and there — that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

[Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence] Craving in the desire realm, craving in the form realm, and craving in the formless realm. [Craving in the formless realm] In the formless realm there is no materiality (dharmas of form), so there is also no body, palace, or physical object; there remains only the mind-consciousness, dwelling in deep and subtle concentration. Its craving is attachment to that deep, subtle concentration, delighting in its agreeableness and giving rise to clinging.
Bhikkhus! But where does this craving arise, and where does it establish itself?
In the world of body and mind, wherever there is something attractive and delightful, there craving arises and establishes itself.
And in the world of body and mind, what are the attractive and delightful things?

Craving is the cause of suffering and the cause of being bound to the round of birth and death. When the six sense faculties come into contact with the six sense objects, the moment the mind gives rise to attachment and longing, this shows that the mind is already bound by the sense fields, and craving has arisen and been established. One should practice at the very place where mind states arise: wherever craving arises, there one should uproot it and extinguish it.

It is the complete abandoning of craving, its cessation, its relinquishing, its renunciation, its release, and its utter non-attachment.

The noble truth of the path explains that by cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path one is able to uproot and extinguish craving wherever it arises, thereby bringing suffering to an end. This is the way of the cessation of suffering. The Amitabha Sūtra says:
“In that land
(the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)

there are always many kinds of wonderful, variegated birds — white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāri, kalaviṅka, and jīvaka, the two-headed birds of shared life. Throughout the six periods of day and night these birds utter harmonious, graceful sounds. Their song proclaims such dharmas as the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path.”
From this we can see the importance of cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path.

And, monks, what is the noble truth of the path that leads to the cessation of suffering? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

And, monks, what is right view? Monks, right view is the knowledge and vision that knows suffering, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path that leads to the cessation of suffering. Monks, this is right view.

And, monks, what is right intention? Monks, right intention is thought that is free from sensual desire and free from attachment to worldly pleasure, and also thought free from hatred and free from violence. Monks, this is right intention.

And, monks, what is right speech? Monks, right speech is abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter. Monks, this is right speech.
And, monks, what is right action? Monks, right action is abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. Monks, this is right action.

And, monks, what is right livelihood? Monks, right livelihood is when a noble disciple does not earn a living by a wrong way of life but carries on his livelihood in a right way. Monks, this is right livelihood.

And, monks, what is right effort? Monks, a monk resolves, strives energetically, arouses his vigor, and applies himself wholeheartedly to preventing unarisen unwholesome actions and unwholesome states of mind from arising; a monk resolves, strives energetically, arouses his vigor, and applies himself wholeheartedly to abandoning unwholesome actions and unwholesome states of mind that have already arisen; a monk resolves, strives energetically, arouses his vigor, and applies himself wholeheartedly to developing unarisen wholesome actions and wholesome states of mind so that they may arise; a monk resolves, strives energetically, arouses his vigor, and applies himself wholeheartedly to sustaining the wholesome states that have already arisen, keeping them from declining and causing them to grow, mature, and reach full development; monks, this is right effort.

And, monks, what is right mindfulness? Monks, a monk dwells ardently mindful, fully comprehending impermanence, contemplating the body in the body, abandoning craving and aversion toward the world of body and mind; a monk dwells ardently mindful, fully comprehending impermanence, contemplating feeling in feeling, abandoning craving and aversion toward the world of body and mind; a monk dwells ardently mindful, fully comprehending impermanence, contemplating mind in mind, abandoning craving and aversion toward the world of body and mind; a monk dwells ardently mindful, fully comprehending impermanence, contemplating dharmas in dharmas, abandoning craving and aversion toward the world of body and mind; monks, this is right mindfulness.

And, monks, what is right concentration? Monks, a monk, having abandoned craving and unwholesome states of mind, gives rise to a mind free from sensual desire, accompanied by initial and sustained thought and filled with rapture and bliss, and he enters the first absorption; with the stilling of initial and sustained thought he attains inner calm and one-pointedness of mind, producing a mind free from sensual desire and free of initial and sustained thought, filled with rapture and bliss, and he enters the second absorption; after rapture subsides, he dwells in equanimity, fully mindful and clearly comprehending impermanence, and he experiences in his body the bliss that the noble ones call the pleasure born of mindfulness and equanimity, and he enters the third absorption; having forsaken pleasure and pain, with the earlier rapture and grief also having vanished, he accordingly enters the fourth absorption, which is beyond pleasure and pain and is filled with equanimity and mindfulness. Monks, this is right concentration.

(Initial and sustained thought) 'Initial thought' is directed inquiry — the seeking of truth, the first, rudimentary consideration; 'sustained thought' is sustained examining — the deeper, more refined consideration.
Monks, this is the noble truth of the path that leads to the cessation of suffering.
Thus,

he dwells contemplating dharmas in internal dharmas, contemplating dharmas in external dharmas, and at the same time contemplating dharmas in both internal and external dharmas. Therefore he dwells contemplating the arising of dharmas, he dwells contemplating the passing away of dharmas, and he dwells contemplating dharmas both arising and passing away.
Monks, this is how a monk contemplates dharmas in dharmas, that is, how he contemplates dharmas in terms of the four noble truths.
Monks, anyone who, in this way, rightly cultivates the four establishments of mindfulness for seven years can expect one of two fruits: the highest wisdom in this very life
(the fruit of the arhat)
, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of the non-returner
(the fruit of the anāgāmin)

(The four fruits) Practicing the four noble truths yields four fruits: the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the fruit of the arhat. The first fruit, the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), rendered into Chinese as 'one who enters the stream,' means one who has just entered the stream of the noble ones; the second fruit, the once-returner (sakadāgāmi), rendered as 'one who returns once,' means one who, having reached this fruit, passes away to the heavens and lives there as a celestial being for a single lifetime, then returns once more to this world, and after that no longer comes to be reborn in the sense-desire realm; the third fruit, the non-returner (anāgāmin), rendered as 'one who does not return,' means one who, having reached this fruit, is no longer reborn in the sense-desire realm; the fourth fruit, the arhat, rendered as 'the unborn,' means one who, having reached this fruit, is freed from birth and death, no longer receives a future existence, and attains the highest fruit. (The sense-desire realm) The world in which sentient beings possessed of lust and appetite dwell. (The highest wisdom in this very life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of the non-returner) Attaining the fruit of the arhat in this very life; and if the five aggregates still remain, attaining the fruit of the non-returner (the fruit of the anāgāmin).
